topStories.headline: Waymo Robot-Taxi Pulls Itself Over in Outer Richmond After Spotting Ghost Gun on Seat
topStories.dek: Interior cameras flagged a loaded, serialless AR-style rifle; two juveniles were arrested and booked at the Juvenile Justice Center.
topStories.body:
A late-night Waymo ride through Outer Richmond ended in a felony arrest on the morning of September 3, when the autonomous vehicle's cameras detected a firearm and the company alerted 911 dispatch. The incident was detailed in the Richmond District police blotter published October 18 by the Richmond Review, drawn from SFPD records.

According to that account, the vehicle's interior cameras observed a passenger who had placed a firearm on the seat next to him. Waymo notified emergency services, and officers from Richmond Station conducted a high-risk felony stop on the 800 block of 40th Avenue, taking both passengers into custody without incident. The firearm recovered was a ghost gun — it bore no serial number or manufacturer markings.

One passenger was booked at the Juvenile Justice Center on a loaded firearms charge; the other was also booked there on a charge of unlawful possession of bear spray. SFPD confirmed the case remains open and active. The San Francisco Chronicle, citing the department, reported that officers also recovered suspected marijuana from inside the vehicle.

Waymo later acknowledged to multiple outlets that one of its fleet vehicles was involved, and said the company cooperated fully with police after detecting what it described as a violation of its terms of service involving a firearm. The company has not publicly said exactly which mechanism — automated system, employee camera review, or another process — first flagged the weapon. It was not the first time a Waymo vehicle in the Bay Area prompted a police call involving juvenile passengers: in July, Waymo alerted San Mateo police after two teenagers were found drinking alcohol and discharging toy firearms in the back of one of its cars.

topStories.headline: After the Anza and Arguello Death, SFMTA Says Protected Designs Are Still Months Away
topStories.dek: The agency told advocates it needs two more months to vet protected-intersection designs for Arguello — three years after state money was secured and construction was supposed to begin.
topStories.body:
The death of 80-year-old Yuan Jun Zhu, struck by a tow truck at Anza Street and Arguello Boulevard on September 28, has drawn fresh attention to a funded street-safety project for that corridor that has stalled repeatedly over more than three years. The pedestrian fatality was reported in last week's issue; this week, the full picture of the safety project's prolonged delay has come into sharper focus.

SFMTA's Livable Streets program manager told advocates in an email dated September 30 that the agency is currently developing designs for protected bicycle corners at multiple intersections along Arguello and will vet them through interagency review over the next two months. After that review, proposed designs would go to a public hearing before any construction plan is finalized. As Streetsblog San Francisco reported, the state funding secured for the project remains unspent.

The corridor's safety history is long and grim. The stretch of Arguello north of Geary remains on SFMTA's High Injury Network even after safety improvements removed other portions of the road from that designation. In 2023, following the death of cyclist Ethan Boyes on Arguello, state Assemblymember Phil Ting secured $1.25 million in state funds for protected bike lanes; District 1 Supervisor Connie Chan and then-District 2 Supervisor Catherine Stefani each pledged an additional $50,000 from community funds. SFMTA initially committed to completing construction by winter 2023, then revised that target to fall/winter 2024. Neither deadline was met.

In a message forwarded to advocates after the September 28 fatality, Supervisor Chan called it heartbreaking and said she remains committed to seeing the project through. Advocates with Streets Forward renewed calls on the mayor and city officials to act, arguing that repeated delays on a fully funded project have cost lives on the same block more than once.

topStories.headline: A Shuttered Geary Car Wash Could Become an 87-Foot Apartment Building
topStories.dek: Permits filed October 9 call for 38 for-sale units at Collins and Geary, the latest mid-rise proposal along the Inner Richmond's main corridor.
topStories.body:
A former self-service car wash at the corner of Collins Street and Geary Boulevard in the Inner Richmond is the site of the neighborhood's latest housing proposal: an eight-story, 38-unit residential building. Permits were filed with the city on October 9, according to SF YIMBY and Hoodline.

The 228 Collins LLC project — with Tim Brown listed as property owner and Kerman Morris Architects responsible for the design — would rise 87 feet on a 0.11-acre parcel. The plan calls for 38 for-sale apartments comprising 18 one-bedrooms, 19 two-bedrooms, and one three-bedroom unit, above a small 300-square-foot ground-floor retail space. Eleven car parking spaces and 38 bicycle spaces are also included in the proposal.

The application invokes the State Density Bonus Law and Senate Bill 330, requesting a 24.5 percent density bonus above base zoning along with waivers covering building height, open space, and facade articulation. Four of the 38 units would be deed-restricted affordable housing for households earning around 80 percent of area median income. The project is at the permit-filing stage and no hearing date has been set.

The proposal joins a string of recent mid-rise filings along Geary. San Francisco faces a state mandate to plan for more than 80,000 new housing units by 2031, and the Inner Richmond — historically low-rise — has drawn increasing developer interest as state density laws enable taller infill on underused parcels like former gas stations and car washes.

moreNews.headline: Presidio Trust CEO Expected Out by Year-End as New Board Settles In
moreNews.body: Jean Fraser, who has led the Presidio Trust since 2016, announced in February that she would step down by end of 2026. The search for her successor was paused in April after President Trump fired the entire Biden-appointed board; in May the White House named six new members, including Time co-chair Lynne Benioff, tech entrepreneur and former U.S. ambassador to Austria Trevor Traina, xAI general counsel James Burnham, and Stanford educator Laura Arrillaga-Andreessen. The Presidio Trust's official website still lists Fraser as CEO as of this week. A spokesperson said in April she would remain until the new board is fully oriented. The park is operating normally, with its full schedule of public events and ranger programs continuing through the fall.

artEntertainment.name: Avenue 12 Gallery
artEntertainment.description: Small Inner Richmond gallery active in the Bay Area arts community, exhibiting local artists and Bay Area subject matter.
